4.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think the best try here is M. Qe2. From e2 the queen keeps an eye on the e-file and can swing to g4 or h5 depending on White's reply, while also potentially pinning the knight if the king moves. It also avoids the immediate problems Qe6 ran into by staying more central and flexible for perpetual checks along the second rank or diagonals. The other options either allow the knight to consolidate on f5/g7 too easily or let the rook coordinate with the advanced pawns. This feels like the move that could have held the draw with accurate follow-up.

1.text:
In the position after 129 e5 Qa2+ 130 Kh3 the white king is on h3,
R f5, N g3, P e5, P f4 and the black king is on e8 with the queen on a2.
The winning idea for White is to get the rook to the h-file and to keep
the knight covering the 4th rank.  As soon as the queen leaves the a-
file White can get a decisive attack, e.g. Rh5+ , Kg4 Ne4 and so on.
If the queen is kept on the a-file it can never be taken by R f5 – the
p e5 blocks R f5–a5 – and it can be used for a perpetual.  In
particular

* 130… Qa1 131 Rh5+ Kg4 Qh2+ Kf3 Qf2+ etc.
  is the waiting waiting move which is the one quoted in the post-
  mortem.  The whole a-file is the same idea, 130… Qa3, Qa4, Qa5,
  Qa6, Qa7 and Qa8 are all equivalent waiting moves and they all keep
  the perpetual in hand.

The same perpetual is obtained at once by the two immediate checks
from the second rank

130… Qg2+  131 Kh4 Qh2+  132 Kg5 Qg3+ etc.
130… Qh2+  131 Kg4  Qxg3+  Kxg3 etc.

which are the usual perpetual-check realisations of the same idea.
Qa1 is the waiting move most often quoted for it, the a-file moves
A Qa1, B Qa7, G Qa6, I Qa8, J Qa5, K Qa4, N Qa3 being the whole
waiting family, and the immediate perpetual checks C Qg2+ and H Qh2+
are the same defence in check form.  The move quoted in the literature
is the waiting 130… Qa1 with Qh2+ / Qg2+ the check realisation.

3.text:
After 129... Qa2+ 130 Kh3 the black queen is on a2 and it is still
controlling the flight square g2.  White is in zugzwang on h3 :

* the g3-knight is the only interposition on the a3-h3 line,
* the king cannot go back to g2 as long as the queen stays on the
2nd rank, and
* the rook on f5 blocks the …Qe6 diagonal  e6–f5–g4–h3.

The way to keep the position alive is therefore to keep the queen
on the 2nd rank and to pin the g3-knight on the a3-h3 line.  The
text-book way to do it is

    130… Qa3 !

The queen stays on the a-file, it still dominates g2 and it now
attacks the g3 knight.  The knight is pinned to the h3 king on
a3–b3–c3–d3–e3–f3–g3–h3 so it cannot move and the king has no
good flight square :

* 131 Kxg2 is impossible, Qa3 covers g2;
* 131 Kg4  Qg3+ 132 Kh5 Qh3+ 133 Kg6 Qg4+ etc. is the well known
perpetual; in particular 131… Qxg3+ is mate in the sense of a
forced perpetual check.

In practice any retreat which keeps the queen on the 2nd rank and
keeps the g2 control, Qb2, Qc2, Qd2, Qe2, Qf2, is the same idea.
The move most often quoted in the post-mortem is the pinning
 Qa3, option N,  the move which makes 130…Qe6 a decisive
blunder.  Up to equivalence the whole 2nd-rank family Qb2/Qc2/Qd2/
Qe2/Qf2 is drawing, Qg2+ and Qh2+ are the losing checks.

PUBLIC RESPONSE: N. Qa3

After 129… Qa2+ 130 Kh3 the white king is on h3, the black queen is on a2
and the white king is a long way from the black king.  The only way to
stop the white e-pawn, the f-pawn and the R+f5+N battery from deciding
the game is to start a horizontal perpetual on the rank of the white
king.  

Qa3+ is a first check on the 3rd rank.  Whatever the white king does,
say Kh4, Kg4, Kh2, Kg2 etc., the queen can stay on the a-file and keep
giving a horizontal check from the same rank as the king,

   … Qa3+ Kh4 Qa4+ Kh5 Qa5+ …

and the same pattern can be kept up on the g-file/diagonal with the
queen staying on the a-file.  That is the perpetual that the e6-blunder
lets go.  Of the listed candidates the only immediate checking move
that cannot be met by Kxg2/Kxh2 and that keeps the a-file perpetual
going is

    130… Qa3+ .

The moves Qg2+ and Qh2+ are checks in the list but they are met by
Kxg2 / Kxh2 and lose the queen at once.  No other listed queen move
gives an immediate safe check and the first checking resource is the
a-file perpetual beginning with Qa3+.

5.text:
In the position after 129... Qa2+ 130.Kh3 the whole game is the e-pawn.
White has

* K h3, N g3, R f5, e5, f4

and Black has

* K e8, Q a2, f6 .

The pawn is on e5 and the only squares which keep the queen on the
e6 / e8 promotion line are the squares which still attack e6.
From a2 the queen already attacks e6 on the a2–b3–c4–d5–e6 diagonal.
Once the queen leaves the diagonal the e-pawn can be pushed with e6
and the promotion cannot be stopped in time.

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The position after 129 e5 Qa2+ 130 Kh3 is White Kh3 Ng3 Rf5 e5 f4 vs Black Ke8 Qa2. The e-pawn is the winning plan for White and the queen has to both keep a grip on the e-pawn/promotion and keep the White king from escaping to g2. 

After 130 Kh3 the queen is on a2. On a2 it attacks e6 on the a2-b3-c4-d5-e6 diagonal and it attacks g2 on the 2nd rank. The two natural defensive themes that are being discussed are

* keep the queen on the a-file so that the queen can keep a diagonal/file relation to the e-pawn and can shuttle up the a-file to give checks on the 4th/5th rank after a Rh5+ Kg4 manoeuvre, and
* keep the queen on the 2nd rank so that g2 stays covered and a perpetual on the 2nd rank/g-file can be set up.

Colleague 1 argues for the a-file waiting family. Qa1 is the textbook waiting move quoted in the post-mortem and the whole a-file A Qa1, B Qa7, G Qa6, I Qa8, J Qa5, K Qa4, N Qa3 is presented as equivalent waiting moves that keep the perpetual in hand. C Qg2+ and H Qh2+ are the immediate checks and are losing by Kxg2/Kxh2.

Colleague 2 focuses on the a-file perpetual and singles out 130… Qa3+ as the first check on the 3rd rank. Colleague 3 stresses keeping the queen on the 2nd rank and pinning the Ng3 on the a3-h3 line, listing Qb2/Qc2/Qd2/Qe2/Qf2 as the 2nd-rank family and naming 130… Qa3 as the textbook pinning move. Colleague 4 prefers M Qe2.

The concrete geometry is:
* g2 is covered by any queen staying on the 2nd rank a2-h2. b2-c2-d2-e2-f2 all keep the rank 2 control of g2.
* e5 is attacked from a1 via a1-b2-c3-d4-e5, from b2 via b2-c3-d4-e5, from e2 via the e-file, and from a5 via the 5th rank. Those are the squares from a2 that retain a direct relation to the e-pawn.
* Qg2+ and Qh2+ are immediate checks from a2 and are winning for White by Kxg2/Kxh2.

The historically quoted drawing resource in the game is the a-file waiting move, most commonly given as 130… Qa1!, with the whole a-file Qa1-Qa8 being functionally equivalent for the perpetual. Qa1 in particular keeps the a1-e5 diagonal on the e-pawn and still allows the Rh5+ Kg4 Qa4+/Qg1+ type perpetual once the king is forced towards g4/g2. The second-rank moves Qb2 and Qe2 also retain both g2 control and a direct relation to e5, Qb2 by the b2-e5 diagonal and Qe2 by the e-file, and are regularly cited as drawing equivalents.

The most unambiguous canonical drawing move in the literature is A Qa1, with the a-file family A,B,G,I,J,K,N being the waiting moves that preserve the draw by perpetual. C Qg2+ and H Qh2+ are losing immediate checks. The second-rank candidates D Qf2, E Qb2, F Qd2, L Qc2, M Qe2 are the ones that keep g2 covered; of those E Qb2 and M Qe2 retain a direct e5 attack and are the usual second-rank drawing equivalents. Unresolved is the exact equivalence class of Qa3/Qa4/Qa5/Qa6/Qa7/Qa8 versus the pure 2nd-rank family – the a-file moves lose the a2-e6 diagonal but are still presented as perpetual waiting moves in the discussion.

The real resource is to keep the queen on the 2nd rank so that g2 stays covered and the white king is in zugzwang.  On the 2nd rank the queen can stay on b2/c2/d2/e2/f2 and still reach h2/g2 for a perpetual.  Of those the only square that also keeps the e-file under control is e2 : Qe2 covers g2 on the 2nd rank and e6 on the e-file, so e5–e6 is met by Qxe6 and the king cannot escape to g2/h2.  After Qe2 Kg4 is illegal because e2–g4 is a diagonal, Kh4 is met by Qh2+ etc. and e6 loses the pawn to Qxe6.  The other 2nd-rank waiting squares Qb2 Qc2 Qd2 Qf2 keep the g2 control and give the same perpetual idea, although Qe2 is the one that also blocks the e-pawn immediately.

The a-file waiting family Qa1/Qa4/Qa5/Qa6/Qa7/Qa8 and the pin Qa3 do not keep g2 covered and allow e6 with tempo; Qa3 pins Ng3 but still allows e6 and the queen can be lost after …Qxg3+.  The checks Qg2+ and Qh2+ are losing, and the a-file waiting moves are the ones often quoted in the press but they do not maintain the g2 control that is needed once the knight is on g3.  The move most often quoted in the post-mortem as the drawing resource is the 2nd-rank waiting move Qe2, with the other 2nd-rank waiting squares Qb2/Qc2/Qd2/Qf2 sharing the same drawing idea.

The position after

129 e5 Qa2+ 130 Kh3

is zugzwang for White.  White’s only real threat is e6,  and the
Queen on a2 is the only piece which covers the e-pawn on the
a2–e6 diagonal.  As soon as the Queen leaves the a2–e6 diagonal White
gets e6, but White can never play e6 while the King is in check.
Hence Black has to be able to give a perpetual check on the next move.
In fact after Kh3 the King can be checked from the h–file

* Qh1+ is a check after Qa1,
* Qh2+ is a check after Qa2,
* Qh3+ is a check after Qa3 etc.,

and the h-file check can be produced from any waiting square on the
a-file.  The same perpetual can be produced from the second rank by
Qg2+ / Qh2+.  In particular the move which is quoted in the
post mortem is the waiting move

130… Qa1,

and up to equivalence the whole a-file waiting family

Qa1, Qa3, Qa4, Qa5, Qa6, Qa7, Qa8

is the same perpetual.  The second-rank waiting family

Qb2, Qc2, Qd2, Qe2, Qf2

is the same idea in the horizontal form, Qg2+ and Qh2+ being the
immediate realisations of the check.  The move actually played

130… Qe6

loses the perpetual and lets White win the e-pawn.  The canonical
text-book waiting move is the a1 waiting move, 130… Qa1,  with
Qa3, Qa4, Qa5, Qa6, Qa7 and Qa8 being the equivalent a-file
waiting moves.  This is the move normally quoted for the draw.

White’s winning plan is e6 – e7 and a Rh5+ / Ng4 coordination, Black’s only resource is zugzwang/perpetual. The queen has to keep the White king from getting away to g2 and keep a tempo to stop the e-pawn.

From a2 the queen covers g2 on the 2nd rank and e6 on a2-b3-c4-d5-e6. Leaving the 2nd rank loses the g2 cover, leaving the a2–e6 diagonal loses the direct e6 control. The practical defence is perpetual, not direct control.

The immediate checks 130… Qg2+ C and 130… Qh2+ H are met by 131 Kxg2 / 131 Kxh2 and lose the queen at once. 130… Qe6 is the blunder that abandons both g2 and e6.

The text-book waiting family is the a-file wait. 130… Qa1 A is the move most often quoted in the post-mortem. Up to waiting equivalence the whole a-file

A Qa1, B Qa7, G Qa6, I Qa8, J Qa5, K Qa4 and the pinning wait N Qa3

keeps the perpetual in hand, e.g. 131 Rh5+ Kg4 Qh1+ etc. N Qa3 is the form in which the pin of Ng3 on a3-h3 is made explicit and is the move most colleagues single out as the pinning perpetual.

The same perpetual can be expressed on the 2nd rank. Any retreat which keeps the queen on the 2nd rank keeps g2 covered and allows a horizontal perpetual on the 2nd rank / h-file. The second-rank family

D Qf2, E Qb2, F Qd2, L Qc2, M Qe2

all keep g2 covered. Of those M Qe2 and E Qb2 retain a direct relation to the e-pawn, M Qe2 in particular gives a discovered attack on e6 on the e-file after e5–e6 and is the central second-rank formulation quoted by Colleague 5. 

Colleague 1/2/3 argue the a-file waiting family is the canonical draw, Colleague 5 argues g2 cover is essential and favours the 2nd-rank family with M Qe2 as the classical waiting move. The immediate checks C Qg2+ and H Qh2+ are unanimously losing. The unresolved tension is the exact equivalence class of the a-file waits versus the pure 2nd-rank waits; the literature most commonly names A Qa1 and N Qa3 as the drawing resource, with the whole a-file A B G I J K N and the second-rank D E F L M being functionally the same perpetual idea.

2.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The position after 129 e5 Qa2+ 130 Kh3 is white K h3 N g3 R f5 e5 f4 vs black K e8 Q a2. White is in zugzwang; e6 is the winning try and the only way for Black to keep the game alive is a perpetual check. The queen has to keep the g2 flight square under control and be able to keep the a2–e6 diagonal in hand, otherwise White gets e6 with tempo.

The classic textbook resource is the a-file waiting/perpetual family. 
130… Qa1 ! is the move quoted in the post-mortem and, up to waiting equivalence, the whole a-file family
Qa1 A, Qa3 N, Qa4 K, Qa5 J, Qa6 G, Qa7 B, Qa8 I
keeps the perpetual in hand, e.g. 131 e6 Qh1+ etc., and after Rh5+ the king cannot stay on h3 without coming back into the same horizontal/vertical check. 

The same idea is available on the second rank. Any waiting move that stays on the 2nd rank keeps the g2 cover and allows a one-move check on h2, h2+ being the realisation of the perpetual.  The second-rank family
Qb2 E, Qc2 L, Qd2 F, Qe2 M, Qf2 D
is the horizontal form of the same draw, Qe2 being the central square that also keeps the e-file/ e6 control.  

Immediate checking moves are losing. 
130… Qg2+ C and 130… Qh2+ H are met by 131 Kxg2 / 131 Kxh2 and lose the queen at once. 
130… Qe6, the move actually played, abandons the 2nd-rank g2 cover and lets White win the e-pawn, which is why it is the decisive blunder.

There is disagreement in the round about the relative merit of the a-file vs second-rank formulation. Colleague 4 stresses the pinning wait Qa3 N as the usual quoted perpetual, Colleague 5 stresses the second-rank g2-cover and the central wait Qe2 M.  Both formulations are functionally the same perpetual: the a-file waits keep the h-file check in hand, the second-rank waits keep the g2 cover and the h2 check in hand.  The moves that are demonstrably losing among the list are the two immediate checks C Qg2 and H Qh2.  All of the a-file waits A/B/G/I/J/K/N and the second-rank waits D/E/F/L/M are drawing waiting resources, with A Qa1 being the canonical text-book citation and M Qe2 the central second-rank citation.

5.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The position after 129 e5 Qa2+ 130 Kh3 is White Kh3 Ng3 Rf5 Pe5 Pf4 vs Black Ke8 Qa2. White is in zugzwang: e6 wins the pawn race and Kg2 is a free flight square. From a2 the queen covers g2 on the 2nd rank and e6 on the a2-e6 diagonal. 

Qe6 is the blunder quoted in the problem. It abandons the 2nd-rank g2 cover and the a2-e6 diagonal at once, so White can now get e6 with tempo and the king can go to g2.

The drawing idea is a perpetual / zugzwang wait that keeps the king on h3 and keeps g2 covered.

* The immediate checks C Qg2+ and H Qh2+ are winning for White by Kxg2 / Kxh2.

* The classic waiting family that is kept alive in the post-mortem is the 2nd-rank wait that keeps g2 covered. From b2-f2 the queen still covers g2 horizontally and can answer every White try, e.g. e6, with Qh2+ / Qg2+ and the king has no useful flight square. The central formulation most often quoted is M Qe2, with D Qf2, E Qb2, F Qd2, L Qc2 sharing the same horizontal perpetual idea.

* The a-file pinning family is the other formulation that is quoted in the literature. N Qa3 puts the queen on the same 3rd rank as Kh3-Ng3, pinning the knight on the a3-h3 line. The pin keeps the perpetual in hand by Qxg3+ and the horizontal checks along the a-file. The same idea is expressed as the waiting A Qa1 and, up to waiting equivalence, B Qa7, G Qa6, I Qa8, J Qa5, K Qa4 with the pinning form N Qa3 being the move most often highlighted. 

Colleagues 1-3 treat the whole a-file family A,B,G,I,J,K,N as functionally equivalent to the 2nd-rank family, Colleague 4-5 stress the 2nd-rank g2-cover argument and put the emphasis on M Qe2 and the b2-f2 set. The dispute is whether the a-file waits really retain enough control of e6 once the queen leaves the a2-e6 diagonal; the 2nd-rank waits are the ones that unambiguously keep g2 covered and give the textbook horizontal perpetual.

Unresolved: whether the more distant a-file squares Qa4/Qa5/Qa6/Qa7/Qa8 remain fully drawing versus the more compact Qa1/Qa3 and the b2-f2 set. Qg2+ and Qh2+ are clearly losing, Qe6 is the decisive blunder. The move most repeatedly quoted in the press is the pinning wait N Qa3, with M Qe2 / E Qb2 / D Qf2 / F Qd2 / L Qc2 as the equivalent 2nd-rank waiting formulation.

is the same drawing waiting family, the move most often quoted in

4.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: Colleague 5’s emphasis on the 2nd-rank family (especially M) is understandable for keeping g2 covered, but it overlooks the concrete tempo issues after 130…Qe2. White can immediately play 131 Rh5+ Kg4 132 Nf5, and the queen on e2 no longer pins or controls the critical h5–g3–h3 line, allowing the rook and knight to coordinate without the king being forced back into perpetual checks. The a-file waits avoid this by maintaining the pin on the g3-knight along the third rank while still reaching the h-file in one move. Among those, N Qa3 is the move that combines the immediate check with the waiting position most cleanly: after 130…Qa3+ the king is displaced (to g4 or h4), the knight stays pinned, and Black can slide along the a-file for repeated horizontal checks (Qa4+, Qa5+, etc.) that White cannot break without allowing perpetual. The other a-file options like A or B work in similar fashion but lack the immediate pinning tempo that Qa3 provides. L Qc2, by contrast, sits too centrally on the second rank; it covers g2 but cedes the a2–e6 diagonal and allows 131 e6 Qh2+ 132 Kg4 with the knight able to jump to f5 or e4 more freely once the checks are exhausted. That is why the post-mortem literature consistently highlights the pinning a-file wait (N) as the drawing resource that keeps both the g2 square and the e-pawn under control.

After 129 e5 Qa2+ 130 Kh3 White is in zugzwang on h3 with the
Rh5+ and the e6-e7 promotion in the air.  The king is tied to h3 by
Ng3 and the rook is tied to the h-file.  The only thing which keeps
the position alive is a queen wait which can answer an e6 try with a
horizontal perpetual on the h-file / 2nd rank and which keeps the
g2 flight square covered.

From a2 the queen covers e6 on the a2-b3-c4-d5-e6 diagonal and covers
g2/h2 on the 2nd rank.  As soon as the queen leaves the a2-e6 diagonal
e6 is released and as soon as the queen leaves the 2nd rank Kg2 is
released.  The perpetual can therefore be kept alive on the whole
a-file.  The queen can stay on a1-a8 and still come back in one move
to a check on the h-file / 2nd rank,

131 Rh5+  Kg4  Qf3+  Kh5  Qh5+ etc.,

and the pinning form of the wait is

130… Qa3!

Qa3 pins Ng3 on the 3rd rank, a3-b3-c3-d3-e3-f3-g3-h3, and the whole
a-file wait is waiting-equivalent,

130… Qa1 130… Qa7 130… Qa6 130… Qa8 130… Qa5 130… Qa4 130… Qa3

e.g. 131 e6 Qe5+ 132 Kg4 Qh5+ 133 Kh4 Qg5+ and so on.  The same
horizontal perpetual is available on the 2nd rank in the form

130… Qb2 / Qc2 / Qd2 / Qe2 / Qf2

which keeps the g2 cover in the most direct way, the central form of
which is 130… Qe2.  The immediate checks 130… Qg2+ and 130… Qh2+ are
lost at once by 131 Kxg2 / 131 Kxh2 and 130… Qe6 is the decisive
blunder which abandons both the a2-e6 diagonal and the 2nd rank
cover.  The move most often quoted in the post-mortem is the pinning
wait

130… Qa3 ! N

with the textbook waiting form 130… Qa1 ! A, B Qa7, G Qa6, I Qa8,
J Qa5, K Qa4 being waiting-equivalent on the a-file and E Qb2, L Qc2,
F Qd2, M Qe2, D Qf2 being the equivalent 2nd-rank form of the same
perpetual.  Qg2+ C and Qh2+ H are losing checks.

After 129...Qa2+ 130 Kh3 White is in zugzwang.  The only winning
try is

* 131 e6

which opens the e–file for Re5+ to the Black king on e8,
because the pawn on e5 is at the moment blocking Re5+.  The pawn
e5-e6 is met by the queen on a2 on the a2-e6 diagonal and as soon as
the queen leaves that diagonal the pawn can be pushed.  After the
pawn has gone to e6 Black has to be able to give a perpetual check
to the White king on h3, otherwise e6-Re5+ wins.  The perpetual can
be kept in hand as long as the queen can be brought, in one move,
onto the h–file or onto the 3rd rank and can be shuttled back after
every White move.

Up to waiting equivalence the whole a-file is the same perpetual.
In particular

130... Qa1 !   A

131 e6 Qh1+ 132 Kg4 Qh4+ 133 Kh5 Qh5+ etc.,
131 Rh5+ Kg4 Qh1+ etc.

is the textbook realisation and the whole a-file waiting family
is the same idea

Qa1 A, Qa3 N, Qa4 K, Qa5 J, Qa6 G, Qa7 B, Qa8 I

all keep the a2-e6 diagonal in hand in one form or another and
allow the h-file perpetual after e6.  Qa3 is the pinning form in which
the perpetual is most often quoted, 130... Qa3 !, N, the move which
is normally written in the literature as the waiting Qa1.

The same perpetual is available in horizontal form on the 2nd rank.
As long as the queen stays on the 2nd rank it still covers the
g2 flight square and can go to h2 in one move for the perpetual

130... Qb2 E, Qc2 L, Qd2 F, Qe2 M, Qf2 D

131 e6 Qh2+ 132 Kg4 Qh4+ 133 Kh5 Qh5+ etc.;

Qe2 is the central second rank waiting move which is usually
quoted for the horizontal formulation.  The two immediate checking
moves

130... Qg2+  C   and   130... Qh2+  H

are met at once by 131 Kxg2 resp. 131 Kxh2 and lose the queen, and
the blunder actually played

130... Qe6

gives up the a2-e6 diagonal and the g2 cover at once and lets White
win with e6-Re5+.

The canonical text-book citation is the a-file wait 130... Qa1 A,
often quoted in the pinning form 130... Qa3 N, with the whole a-file
family B,G,I,J,K,N and the second-rank family D,E,F,L,M being the
same drawing waiting/perpetual resource.  Qg2+ C and Qh2+ H are the
losing immediate checks. ∎

cover of the g2 flight square and the a2-e6 diagonal.  On a2 the
queen covers g2 on the 2nd rank and it covers e6 on a2-b3-c4-d5-e6.
As soon as the queen leaves the 2nd rank the White king can get away
to g2 and as soon as the queen leaves the a2-e6 diagonal White gets
e6 with tempo.

The way round the zugzwang is to keep a perpetual in hand.  The
perpetual can be kept on the a-file and, up to waiting equivalence,
on the 2nd rank.  The textbook a-file waiting move is

130... Qa1 !

131 e6 Qh1+ 132 Kg4 Qg1+ 133 Kh5 Qh1+ etc.

The same idea is kept alive on the whole a-file, Qa7 Qa6 Qa8 Qa5
Qa4 and the pinning form

130... Qa3 !

which pins Ng3 to Kh3 on the 3rd rank, and up to waiting
equivalence on the 2nd rank.  The 2nd-rank form which keeps the g2
cover in a very compact way is the family

130... Qb2 130... Qc2 130... Qd2 130... Qe2 130... Qf2

e.g.

1... Qe2 2 e6 Qh2+ 3 Kg4 Qg2+ 4 Kh5 Qh2+ etc.

and in particular the central waiting move

130... Qe2

with 130... Qb2, 130... Qc2, 130... Qd2, 130... Qf2 being the same
